people.name: George Latimer
body: In 1975 a labor lawyer who had served on St. Paul's school board entered the race for mayor. In 1976 he won by about 2,200 votes over a former mayor. He served about 14 years, until he declined to seek a seventh term in 1989, and became the longest-serving mayor in the city's history.

George Latimer was born in Poughkeepsie, New York, in June 1935 and grew up in Schenectady, New York. His mother was a Catholic of Lebanese descent and his father a Protestant of English descent. Families like his mother's were part of a large emigration from Mount Lebanon, then under Ottoman rule, from the late 1800s through the early 1900s. Some of them settled on the West Side of St. Paul and in Northeast Minneapolis, where their parishes still operate or have moved nearby.

Latimer came to St. Paul and built a law practice focused on labor and union issues. He was elected to the St. Paul School Board in 1970 and was a University of Minnesota regent when he ran for mayor. During his years as mayor, from 1976 to 1990, downtown gained the Ordway Center for the Performing Arts and the 38-story Wells Fargo Place, and the Lowertown warehouse district was revived. He also backed District Energy, a shared system of underground pipes that heats and cools buildings downtown and on the West Side. In 1986 he ran for governor and lost the DFL primary to the incumbent, Rudy Perpich.

After City Hall he became dean of Hamline University School of Law, leaving in 1993 for a federal housing post in the Clinton administration, and he stayed active in civic life for decades. In 2014 St. Paul renamed its downtown central library the George Latimer Central Library. He died on August 18, 2024, at age 89.
His legacy shows up in the buildings and systems St. Paul still runs on. In a 1997 Minnesota Public Radio interview he spoke about his Lebanese mother.
keyFacts: June 1935: Born in Poughkeepsie, New York; grew up in Schenectady.
1970: Elected to the St. Paul School Board.
1976: Won election as mayor of St. Paul by about 2,200 votes.
1976–1990: Served as mayor, the longest tenure in city history.
1986: Lost the DFL primary for governor to Rudy Perpich.
2014: St. Paul's central library renamed in his honor.
August 18, 2024: Died at 89.
people.connectToWork: What assumptions about a person's background does your process make from a name? How would you learn what heritage, if any, the person wants you to know about?

people.name: Herb Mocol
body: During the 1952 flood in Mankato, a man from a family grocery on the city's north end used his trucks to help poorer families evacuate. About two decades later, Herb Mocol was mayor of the city.

Mocol's father was a Lebanese immigrant who started Mocol's grocery store on the north end of Mankato. The city's Lebanese community dates to around 1890, when families from Mount Lebanon, then part of the Ottoman Empire, settled in southern Minnesota. Mocol lived within a block of the store for his whole life. His obituary lists him as president of Mocol Super Markets and past president of Mocol Truck Line. In 2005 his sons were still running the store.

According to the Mankato Free Press, he saw inequities in his community from a young age. In the late 1960s he entered politics by leading a petition drive to create city wards. He served four years on the City Council and was elected mayor in 1974, holding the job 12 years, according to his 2005 obituary in the Mankato Free Press. The Blue Earth County Historical Society gives his years as mayor as 1975 to 1986. He was an active member of the DFL Party, where he met Walter Mondale around 1960, and the paper described him as a fiscal conservative and an astute businessman.

As mayor, he was proudest of helping win federal funding for a flood-control project for Mankato and North Mankato. He also helped create a new library with Blue Earth County and oversaw an upgraded swimming pool in Tourtellotte Park. He promoted Lebanese culture, and the paper reported that several organizations listed him among the most influential Lebanese Americans in the country. He and his wife, Jen, raised 11 children. He died on September 27, 2005, at age 82.
keyFacts: April 6, 1923: Born.
1952: Used his trucks to help families evacuate during the Mankato flood.
Late 1960s: Led a petition drive to create city wards.
Served four years on the City Council before becoming mayor.
1974 or 1975 to 1986: Mayor of Mankato. His 2005 obituary says elected 1974, held the job 12 years; the Blue Earth County Historical Society says 1975 to 1986.
As mayor: Won federal funding for flood control; helped create a joint city-county library.
September 27, 2005: Died at 82.
people.connectToWork: When you plan outreach outside the Twin Cities, whose long history in that town are you counting? Who already knows which families were hit hardest the last time something went wrong?

people.name: Michael Henne
body: In 1895, thirty newly arrived Lebanese immigrants were living above a store at 123 Main Street in Minneapolis. The store belonged to Michael Henne, who had come to the city in 1889. By the Northeaster newspaper's account, he spoke English, which helped him succeed, and he sponsored many fellow immigrants, who were then often called Syrians.

By 1905 he had moved to a larger building at 521 Marshall Street, where 51 people lived. He became a wholesaler, giving goods on credit to peddlers who sold them across the state. The same account says most of those peddlers were women, and that one, Sadie Jacobs, traveled as far as Hibbing, sometimes for about a month at a time. By 1918 there were 104 Syrian families in Northeast.
We found only this one account of his life, and it gives no birth or death dates.
keyFacts: 1889: Arrived in Minneapolis.
1895: Thirty newcomers lived above his store at 123 Main St.
1905: Moved to 521 Marshall St., where 51 people lived.
Supplied peddlers with goods on credit.
people.connectToWork: When newcomers rely on a sponsor for housing and credit, what would you want to understand about that arrangement before you judge their living situation or income?

people.name: Huda Zoghbi
body: In 1999 a team in Huda Zoghbi's laboratory in Houston identified mutations in a gene called MECP2 as the cause of Rett syndrome, a severe neurological disorder that mostly affects girls. The finding made a simple genetic test for the condition possible.

Zoghbi was born Huda El-Hibri on June 20, 1954, in Beirut, Lebanon, and grew up there. She entered the American University of Beirut in 1973 and began medical school two years later. When the Lebanese Civil War made study in Beirut impossible, her parents sent her and her brother to stay with a sister in Austin, Texas, expecting them to return the next summer. The war went on. She finished medical school at Meharry Medical College in Nashville, a historically Black medical school, earning her M.D. in 1979.

In 1983 she joined Baylor College of Medicine and Texas Children's Hospital for a child neurology residency. As a clinician she saw children with Rett syndrome and turned to research. In 1993, working with Harry Orr of the University of Minnesota Medical School, she helped identify ATAXIN1, the gene behind spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), an inherited movement disorder. Her later work showed that the amount of MECP2 protein matters: too little causes Rett syndrome and too much causes a different disorder.

She became founding director of the Jan and Dan Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator. Her honors include the Shaw Prize (2016), the Canada Gairdner International Award (2017) and the 2022 Kavli Prize in Neuroscience, which she shared with Orr, Jean-Louis Mandel and Christopher Walsh. Lebanon awarded her its National Order of the Cedar in 2018.
keyFacts: June 20, 1954: Born in Beirut, Lebanon.
1979: M.D., Meharry Medical College, after the civil war interrupted her studies in Beirut.
1993: With Harry Orr of the University of Minnesota, identified ATAXIN1, the SCA1 gene.
1999: Her team identified MECP2 as the cause of Rett syndrome.
2016: Shaw Prize; 2017: Gairdner Award; 2022: Kavli Prize in Neuroscience.
people.connectToWork: When someone's studies or career were cut short by war, how does your process recognize what they already know and can do?

people.name: Danny Thomas
body: Before he was famous, a struggling young entertainer with a baby on the way prayed to St. Jude Thaddeus, the patron saint of hopeless causes. He asked to be shown his way in life and vowed to build the saint a shrine. On February 4, 1962, about 9,000 people gathered in Memphis, Tennessee, for the opening of St. Jude Children's Research Hospital, the shrine he built.

Danny Thomas was born Amos Muzyad Yaqoob Kairouz on January 6, 1912, in Deerfield, Michigan. His parents, Charles Yaqoob Kairouz and Margaret Taouk, were Maronite Catholic immigrants from the area of Bsharri in northern Lebanon. The Maronite Church is an Eastern Catholic church; St. Maron in Northeast Minneapolis belongs to it.

Thomas started on Detroit radio station WMBC in 1932 and, after moving to Chicago in 1940, took the stage name "Danny Thomas," built from the names of two of his brothers. He became a star of radio, film and television. His sitcom Make Room for Daddy, later called The Danny Thomas Show, premiered in 1953 and ran until 1964, when Thomas voluntarily ended it.

He founded St. Jude with help from Dr. Lemuel Diggs and his friend Anthony Abraham, a Miami auto dealer, and turned to fellow Americans of Arabic-speaking descent to fund it: in 1957, 100 representatives of the Arab American community met in Chicago to form ALSAC, the hospital's fundraising organization. In 1983 President Ronald Reagan presented him with a Congressional Gold Medal for that work. He died in Los Angeles on February 6, 1991.
keyFacts: January 6, 1912: Born in Deerfield, Michigan, to Maronite Lebanese immigrants.
1953–1964: Make Room for Daddy / The Danny Thomas Show.
1957: ALSAC formed by 100 Arab American representatives in Chicago to fund the hospital.
February 4, 1962: St. Jude Children's Research Hospital opened in Memphis.
1983: Congressional Gold Medal.
February 6, 1991: Died in Los Angeles.
people.connectToWork: Who in your work has built care that serves people far beyond their own group? How would you find out which people and funders outside government are already holding up the service you depend on?

people.name: Helen Thomas
body: For decades, presidential press conferences closed with the words "Thank you, Mr. President," usually spoken by Helen Thomas, who sat in the front row. She covered ten presidents, from John F. Kennedy to the second year of Barack Obama's presidency.

Thomas was born on August 4, 1920, in Winchester, Kentucky, the seventh of nine children. Her parents, George and Mary Thomas, were immigrants from Tripoli, in what is now Lebanon and was then part of the Ottoman Empire, who had arrived in 1903. Her father could not read or write but ran a successful grocery store. When she was four the family moved to Detroit, which she always considered her hometown.

In 1943 she started as a copy girl at the Washington Daily News and soon joined United Press, later United Press International (UPI), where she stayed 57 years before leaving in 2000. In 1974 she became the first woman to head a wire service's White House bureau. She was the first woman officer of the National Press Club, the first woman president of the White House Correspondents' Association in 1975–76, and in 1975 the first woman member of the Gridiron Club, which she later also led. She died at her Washington, D.C., home on July 20, 2013, at 92.

In her later years she wrote a column for Hearst Newspapers. On May 27, 2010, in an informal videotaped exchange outside the White House, she was asked for comments on Israel and said that Israelis should "get the hell out of Palestine." She apologized in a statement days later, saying she deeply regretted the comments. After the video circulated widely, she retired from Hearst in June 2010.
keyFacts: August 4, 1920: Born in Winchester, Kentucky, to Lebanese immigrants from Tripoli.
1943: Joined United Press (later UPI); stayed 57 years.
1974: First woman to head a wire service's White House bureau.
1975–76: First woman president of the White House Correspondents' Association.
1975: First woman member of the Gridiron Club.
June 2010: Retired from Hearst Newspapers after criticized remarks about Israel, for which she had apologized.
July 20, 2013: Died at 92.
people.connectToWork: Which rooms in your organization are still hard to enter for the first person of their kind? What would you change besides the person's own persistence?

people.name: Michael E. DeBakey
body: While still a medical student in the late 1920s and early 1930s, Michael DeBakey devised a roller pump. The pump later became a key part of the heart-lung machine that made open-heart surgery possible.

DeBakey was born on September 7, 1908, in Lake Charles, Louisiana. His parents, Shaker Morris and Raheeja Debaghi, were Lebanese immigrants, and the family name was later Anglicized. He earned his medical degree in 1932.

During World War II he helped develop the Army's Auxiliary Surgical Groups, first deployed in 1943, which evolved into Mobile Auxiliary Surgical Hospital (MASH) units. He received the Legion of Merit in 1945. After the war, he and Denton Cooley began making artificial arterial grafts from DuPont's new Dacron fabric within several years of a 1952 aneurysm repair. The grafts changed vascular surgery.

He received the Albert Lasker Award for Clinical Research (1963), the Presidential Medal of Freedom (1969), the National Medal of Science (1987) and the Congressional Gold Medal (2008). He died on July 11, 2008, at 99.
keyFacts: September 7, 1908: Born in Lake Charles, Louisiana, to Lebanese immigrant parents.
1932: Earned his M.D.; devised the roller pump as a student.
1943: Auxiliary Surgical Groups first deployed, the forerunners of MASH units.
1969: Presidential Medal of Freedom; 1987: National Medal of Science.
2008: Congressional Gold Medal; died July 11, 2008.
people.connectToWork: Does anything in your process read an anglicized or changed family name as a discrepancy? How would you record it without treating the person as suspect?

people.name: Donna Shalala
body: In the early 1960s a young woman from Cleveland went to a village in southern Iran as one of the Peace Corps' first volunteers. Three decades later, Donna Shalala became the first Lebanese American to serve in a U.S. Cabinet.

Shalala was born on February 14, 1941, in Cleveland, Ohio, to parents of Maronite Catholic Lebanese descent. After graduating from Western College for Women in 1962 she spent two years in Iran with the Peace Corps, then built a career in academic leadership. She became president of Hunter College in New York in 1980, and in the late 1980s she moved to the University of Wisconsin–Madison, a neighbor to Minnesota's university system, where she was chancellor until 1993.

President Bill Clinton appointed her Secretary of Health and Human Services, and she served the full eight years, from 1993 to 2001. She then led the University of Miami from 2001 to 2015. In 2008 President George W. Bush awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Later she was elected to Congress and represented Florida's 27th District from 2019 to 2021.
keyFacts: February 14, 1941: Born in Cleveland, Ohio.
1962: Graduated from Western College for Women, then spent two years as a Peace Corps volunteer in Iran.
Until 1993: Chancellor, University of Wisconsin–Madison.
1993–2001: U.S. Secretary of Health and Human Services, the first Lebanese American Cabinet member.
2008: Presidential Medal of Freedom; 2019–2021: U.S. Representative from Florida.
people.connectToWork: If you were leading the agency that sets the rules you work under, whose experience would you want at the table before the rule was written?

people.name: Ray LaHood
body: As U.S. Secretary of Transportation, Ray LaHood made distracted driving his signature cause. He warned again and again about texting and phone use behind the wheel and released videos of people who had lost loved ones in crashes where distraction played a role. Near the end of his time in office he called this campaign the accomplishment that was most his own.

LaHood was born on December 6, 1945, in Peoria, Illinois. His parents, Ed and Mary, ran a working-class restaurant and tavern on the city's Southwest Jefferson Street, and his grandparents had emigrated from Lebanon to Peoria in 1895. He worked his way through Canton Junior College and Bradley University, earned a bachelor's degree in education and sociology from Bradley in 1971, and taught junior high social studies in Pekin and Peoria for six years.

He moved into politics through staff work for Congressman Tom Railsback, a short 1982 appointment to the Illinois House, and then the staff of House Republican Leader Robert Michel, whose district offices he ran before becoming Michel's chief of staff in 1990. When Michel retired, LaHood won the seat and represented Illinois's 18th District in the U.S. House from 1995 to 2009. In 2009 President Barack Obama, a Democrat, chose LaHood, a Republican, as the 16th Secretary of Transportation. He took office on January 23, 2009, and left the department in July 2013.
keyFacts: December 6, 1945: Born in Peoria, Illinois; grandparents emigrated from Lebanon to Peoria in 1895.
1971: B.S., Bradley University; then taught junior high social studies for six years.
1983–1994: On the staff of House Republican Leader Robert Michel, as chief of staff from 1990.
1995–2009: U.S. Representative, Illinois's 18th District.
2009–2013: 16th U.S. Secretary of Transportation under President Obama; led a national campaign against distracted driving.
people.connectToWork: When a safety or service campaign reaches everyone, how do you check that the people most affected helped shape the message and can get it in a form they can use?

people.name: Ralph Nader
body: In November 1965 a young Connecticut lawyer published a book arguing that American cars were designed in ways that put people's lives at risk. The book was Unsafe at Any Speed, and its sharpest criticism was aimed at General Motors' Chevrolet Corvair. The next year Congress passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act of 1966. It gave the federal government the power to set safety standards for every car sold in the United States.
Ralph Nader was born on February 27, 1934, in Winsted, Connecticut. His parents, Nathra and Rose Nader, were Antiochian Orthodox Christian immigrants from Mount Lebanon.

He graduated from Princeton in 1955 and earned his law degree at Harvard in 1958. In 1964 he was a consultant to the U.S. Department of Labor. After his book made him a national figure, he built a network of advocacy and watchdog organizations, among them Public Citizen, which he founded in 1971, and the Public Interest Research Groups. By the accounts of Arab America and CNN, he played a part in the creation of the Freedom of Information Act and the Consumer Product Safety Commission, and lobbied for the Wholesome Meat Act of 1967 and the 1970 law that created the Occupational Safety and Health Administration. In 1988 he was instrumental in passing California's Proposition 103, which rolled back auto insurance rates.

Nader ran for president four times: as the Green Party's nominee in 1996 and 2000, when he received nearly three million votes, and as an independent in 2004 and 2008. In 2014 he launched the Ralph Nader Radio Hour, and in 2015 the American Museum of Tort Law opened in his hometown of Winsted.
keyFacts: February 27, 1934: Born in Winsted, Connecticut, to Lebanese immigrant parents.
1955: Graduated from Princeton; 1958: Graduated from Harvard Law School.
1965: Published Unsafe at Any Speed; 1966: National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act passed.
1971: Founded Public Citizen.
1988: Helped pass California's Proposition 103.
1996, 2000: Green Party presidential nominee; 2004, 2008: Ran as an independent.
2015: American Museum of Tort Law opened in Winsted.
people.connectToWork: Where does your process wait for a harm to be proven before it changes? Who is in a position to tell you about a design problem before someone is hurt?

people.name: Casey Kasem
body: On July 4, 1970, a new radio countdown show began in Los Angeles. The host, Casey Kasem, made American Top 40 a weekly ritual, and his became one of the best-known voices in America.

Kasem was born Kemal Amin Kasem on April 27, 1932, in Detroit, Michigan. His parents, Amin and Helen Kasem, were Lebanese Druze immigrants who worked as grocers. The Druze are a religious community with deep roots in Lebanon's mountains. Lebanese Americans include Christian, Muslim and Druze families, and a name or a place of origin does not tell you which.

Kasem was also a prolific voice actor. Beginning in 1969 with Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!, he was the first actor to voice Shaggy Rogers, a role he kept for about 40 years. He stepped down from American Top 40 in 2004, and in 2009 he retired from radio and voice acting.

He spoke openly about his heritage. In a 1983 interview, he said he wanted people to know that he was Lebanese and Arab. By the account of ACCESS, an Arab American human services organization in Michigan, he fought media stereotyping of Arabs and Arab Americans, encouraged young Arab American media producers and gave to Arab American causes, including a fellowship in Druze and Arab Studies at Georgetown University. He served on the honorary National Advisory Board of the Arab American National Museum in Dearborn, Michigan, from its opening in 2005. He lent his voice to one of its exhibits and donated his Hollywood Walk of Fame plaque. He died on June 15, 2014, in Gig Harbor, Washington, at 82.
keyFacts: April 27, 1932: Born Kemal Amin Kasem in Detroit to Lebanese Druze parents.
1969: Began voicing Shaggy in Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!, a role he held for about 40 years.
July 4, 1970: American Top 40 debuted.
2004: Stepped down from American Top 40; 2009: Retired from radio and voice acting.
2005: Honorary member of the Arab American National Museum's National Advisory Board.
June 15, 2014: Died in Gig Harbor, Washington, at 82.
people.connectToWork: What images of Arabs or Arab Americans are in the training, media or examples your team uses? Who has checked them, and what would you do if someone told you one was wrong?

people.name: Kahlil Gibran
body: In 1923 a slim book of poetic essays appeared in New York. In it, a wise man named Almustafa answers questions about love, work, children, freedom and death. That book was The Prophet, and its author, Kahlil Gibran, is one of the best-known Lebanese-born writers in the world.

Gibran was born on January 6, 1883, in Bsharri, a mountain village in northern Lebanon. At the time the area was the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate, a self-governing district of the Ottoman Empire. In June 1895, at age twelve, he sailed to the United States with his mother and siblings, and the family settled in Boston's large Syrian and Lebanese community.

Gibran wrote in both Arabic and English and was also a painter. He lived in New York from 1912 until his death, and there he and other writers of the Arab diaspora, known in Arabic as the mahjar, formed the Arabic-language Pen League, al-Rabita al-Qalamiyya. It grew out of an informal union of émigré writers begun in 1916 and was formally established in April 1920, with Gibran as its founder-president. By his estate's account, he started a Romantic movement in Arabic literature from New York that pushed it toward new, freer forms.

He died of illness on April 10, 1931, at St. Vincent's Hospital in New York, at age 48. As he had wished, his sister Mary brought his coffin back to Bsharri that August, and his remains lie in a crypt at the former Mar Sarkis Monastery, now the Gibran Museum. In 1991 a memorial garden in his honor was dedicated in Washington, D.C.
keyFacts: January 6, 1883: Born in Bsharri, Mount Lebanon (Ottoman Empire).
June 1895: Immigrated at age twelve with his mother and siblings to Boston.
1912–1931: Lived in New York.
April 1920: Pen League formally established, with Gibran as president.
1923: The Prophet published.
April 10, 1931: Died in New York at 48; buried in Bsharri.
people.connectToWork: A person may read, write and create in more than one language. How does your process find out which language someone wants to use for which purpose, rather than recording just one?

people.name: Philip Habib
body: In the summer of 1982, Beirut was under siege, with fighters of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) trapped in the city. President Ronald Reagan's special envoy, Philip Habib, the son of Lebanese immigrants, found a formula that ended the fighting and let the PLO forces leave Beirut for other Arab countries. Reagan awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom for his contributions to peace.

Habib was born on February 25, 1920, in Brooklyn, New York, to Lebanese immigrants who had come in the late 1800s: his father from the Sidon area and his mother from a small town north of Beirut. By his own account in an oral history, his father was a Maronite and his mother was not, and the family went to the Maronite church on special occasions. He did not start out to be a diplomat. He studied forestry at the University of Idaho, graduating in 1942, served in the Army in World War II, and then used the G.I. Bill to earn a Ph.D. in agricultural economics at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1952.

He became a career Foreign Service officer and rose to the top of the profession. According to the State Department's Office of the Historian, he was U.S. Ambassador to South Korea from 1971 to 1974, Assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific Affairs from 1974 to 1976, and Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs from 1976 to 1978. For a few days in January 1977, during the change of administrations, he also served as acting Secretary of State.
After retiring, he was called back for the Middle East, including his parents' homeland, then in the middle of the Lebanese Civil War. He died on May 25, 1992, in Puligny-Montrachet, France.
keyFacts: February 25, 1920: Born in Brooklyn to Lebanese immigrant parents.
1942: Graduated in forestry, University of Idaho; 1952: Ph.D., UC Berkeley.
1971–1974: Ambassador to South Korea.
1976–1978: Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs; acting Secretary of State January 20–23, 1977.
1982: As special envoy, negotiated the PLO evacuation from Beirut; Presidential Medal of Freedom.
May 25, 1992: Died in Puligny-Montrachet, France.
people.connectToWork: When you ask a colleague to speak for or deal with people from their family's homeland, what are you assuming about what they know, and what is the cost to them?

people.name: John Abizaid
body: In July 2003, months after the U.S. invasion of Iraq, Army General John Abizaid took command of U.S. Central Command, the headquarters responsible for American forces across the Middle East. He held the post until March 2007, longer than any of his predecessors.
Abizaid was born on April 1, 1951, in northern California. He is the grandson of Lebanese immigrants and was raised Roman Catholic.

He graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1973 and was commissioned as an infantry officer. A fluent Arabic speaker, he earned a master's degree in Middle Eastern studies at Harvard. In 1983, during the U.S. invasion of Grenada, he led an advance using a bulldozer for cover, a scene later depicted in the 1986 film Heartbreak Ridge. He later served as commandant of cadets at West Point and was a fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution.

He retired from the Army on May 1, 2007, after 34 years of service. Nominated in 2018, he returned to public service as U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, the first American ambassador in Riyadh since 2016. He was sworn in in April 2019 and arrived in Riyadh in early May 2019.
keyFacts: April 1, 1951: Born in northern California.
June 1973: Graduated from West Point.
1983: Grenada action later depicted in Heartbreak Ridge (1986).
July 7, 2003–March 16, 2007: Commander, U.S. Central Command.
May 1, 2007: Retired after 34 years.
Nominated 2018; sworn in April 2019: U.S. Ambassador to Saudi Arabia.
people.connectToWork: Language skill and regional study took him years of work. When your team needs language or regional knowledge, are you paying for it and building it, or borrowing it from whoever happens to have it?

people.name: George J. Mitchell
body: On Good Friday 1998, after talks that he chaired, the parties in Northern Ireland reached the Belfast Agreement, better known as the Good Friday Agreement. The chairman of those talks, former U.S. Senate Majority Leader George Mitchell, was the son of a Lebanese immigrant mother.

Mitchell was born on August 20, 1933, in Waterville, Maine. His mother, known as Mary (née Saad), came to the United States from the village of Bkassine, Lebanon, in 1920 at about age eighteen, and worked in Waterville-area textile mills. His father was the orphaned son of Irish immigrants and was adopted by a Lebanese American family; he worked as a laborer and later as a janitor at Colby College. Arab America says Mitchell was raised in Waterville's Lebanese Maronite community.

Trained as a lawyer, he was appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1980 to finish the term of Edmund Muskie, who had become Secretary of State. Maine voters elected him in 1982 and 1988. Senate Democrats chose him as majority leader, and he held that post from 1989 until he retired from the Senate at the start of 1995.

In 1995 President Bill Clinton asked him to lead an international effort on Northern Ireland, and he went on to chair the Northern Ireland peace negotiations. In 1999 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. From 2009 to 2011 he served as President Barack Obama's Special Envoy for Middle East Peace.
keyFacts: August 20, 1933: Born in Waterville, Maine; mother an immigrant from Bkassine, Lebanon.
1980: Appointed to the U.S. Senate; elected 1982 and 1988.
1989–1995: Senate Majority Leader.
1995: Named by Clinton to lead the Northern Ireland effort; chaired the talks that produced the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
1999: Presidential Medal of Freedom.
2009–2011: Special Envoy for Middle East Peace.
people.connectToWork: A family can hold more than one heritage, as his did. When your form asks for one race, ethnicity or language, what do you lose, and how could the person correct it?

people.name: Christa McAuliffe
body: In 1984 NASA began a national search for a civilian who could share a shuttle mission with the public. It chose Christa McAuliffe, a social studies teacher at Concord High School in New Hampshire. According to Arab News, she was selected on recommendations from her students and from fellow teachers around the country who knew her work. On January 28, 1986, she died with six crewmates when the Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart about 73 seconds after liftoff, with the launch broadcast on live television.
According to Arab News, she was the granddaughter of a Lebanese immigrant of Maronite descent and the great-niece of the Lebanese American historian Philip K. Hitti.

In 2021 the U.S. Mint issued a silver dollar in her honor, which Arab News described as the first American coin honoring an Arab American. Its design includes the words "I touch the future. I teach," and $10 from each sale went to the FIRST youth robotics program.
keyFacts: 1984: NASA began its national search for a civilian to fly.
January 28, 1986: Died in the Challenger disaster.
2021: Commemorated on a U.S. silver dollar.

people.name: Sylvana Lakkis
body: Sylvana Lakkis is a Lebanese disability rights advocate based in Lebanon. WISE Muslim Women's profile says she has worked with the Lebanese Physically Handicapped Union (LPHU), later also called the Lebanese Union for People with Physical Disabilities, since 1986, and has been its president since 2001. In a 2003 Oxfam account of the union's advocacy, she is quoted as its president, saying of Lebanon's new government, "We shall give them the benefit of doubt and seek their help and collaboration."

The Arab NGO Network for Development, which published her writing on inclusive reconstruction in June 2026, lists her as chairperson of the union and calls her a co-founder. That title does not match the WISE dates, since the union began in 1981. It also lists her as chair of the Arab Forum for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and as disability advisor to Lebanon's Minister of Social Affairs from 2008 to 2012. Fifty Fifty, a Lebanese women's political participation group, calls her the union's executive director.
keyFacts: 1986: Began work with LPHU, by WISE Muslim Women's account.
2001: Became president, by the same account.
2008–2012: Disability advisor to Lebanon's Minister of Social Affairs.
June 2026: Published on inclusive reconstruction after war.
people.connectToWork: When you need to understand disability in a family's country of origin, are you hearing from disabled leaders or only about them?

people.name: Nawaf Kabbara
body: Nawaf Kabbara is a Lebanese disability leader based in Lebanon and a former associate professor of political science at the University of Balamand. As of October 2026, the International Disability Alliance names him its president, and also president of the National Association for the Rights of Persons with Disabilities in Lebanon and of the Arab Organization of Persons with Disabilities. A Qatar News Agency report from Doha in November 2025 gives him the same Arab Organization title.

Zero Project's 2019 profile credits him with founding the Forum of the Handicapped in 1986 and a national rights association in 1987, with becoming the first person with a disability to run for Lebanon's parliament in 1996, and with helping to found the Arab Organization of Persons with Disabilities in 1998, which he led until 2008. The International Disability Alliance adds that he led a 1987 march by disabled people against the war in Lebanon, took part in negotiating the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and headed the human rights committee of Lebanon's socio-economic council.
keyFacts: 1986: Founded the Forum of the Handicapped.
1987: Led a march by disabled people against the war in Lebanon.
1996: First person with a disability to run for Lebanon's parliament.
As of October 2026: President of the International Disability Alliance.
people.connectToWork: Who are the disabled leaders with power in the decisions you work on? If there are none, what would need to change?

institutions.name: St. Maron Maronite Catholic Church
institutions.type: Place of worship and cultural center
body: On February 9, 1903, the feast day of St. Maron, Lebanese immigrants in Minneapolis gathered in a home at 311 Main Street for the city's first Maronite Mass. By the Northeaster's account, the church became the center of the culture, food and music of Lebanese Northeast.

The congregation grew with the Lebanese community of Northeast Minneapolis, where early settlers such as Michael Henne housed and supplied newcomers. In 1919 the parish acquired an abandoned church at 625 Main Street. By 1939 it had bought the Everett Public School at Sixth Street and University Avenue, and less than ten years later it built a new church on that site. The church today is at 600 University Avenue NE, and by the Northeaster's account it serves Christians from across the Middle East. Chorbishop Sharbel Maroun told CBS Minnesota in 2024 that more than half of his parishioners had immigrated from Lebanon to escape political unrest and economic crisis. On Aug. 28, 2026, the Vatican announced that Pope Leo XIV approved his election as Maronite archbishop of Damascus, Syria. The Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis said he has served St. Maron for more than 35 years and "will be deeply missed."

Early Maronite communities in the United States were served by local Latin bishops. In 1966 Pope Paul VI created a Maronite Apostolic Exarchate for the country; in 1994 the U.S. Maronite diocese was divided in two, and today St. Maron belongs to the Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon while sitting within the territory of the Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis.

The parish also carries Lebanese culture to the wider public. In September 2024 it held its 33rd annual Lebanese Festival, which drew visitors to celebrate food and culture while war was intensifying in Lebanon.
keyFacts: February 9, 1903: First Maronite Mass in Minneapolis, at 311 Main St.
1919: Parish acquired a church at 625 Main St.
By 1939: Bought the Everett School site at Sixth St. and University Ave.; new church built less than ten years later.
1966: Separate Maronite jurisdiction created for the United States.
September 2024: 33rd annual Lebanese Festival.
institutions.connectToWork: Do you know which congregations and neighborhood institutions have been in the area you serve for over a century? How would you begin a relationship with one without treating it as speaking for everyone?

institutions.name: Emily's Lebanese Deli
body: In 1973 Emily Awaijane, who had arrived from Lebanon in 1936, opened a small deli on University Avenue in Northeast Minneapolis, close to St. Maron. More than 50 years later, Emily's Lebanese Deli still serves homemade Lebanese food from the same address and describes itself as a family-owned business.

Awaijane had built bombsights for the U.S. Navy during World War II, worked at a soda fountain and spent years as a banquet waitress downtown. In the 1960s she began preparing food at home for Lebanese buyers. Her son Ron told the Northeaster that most of the deli's customers were neighboring Poles and Ukrainians, not Lebanese.

The deli sits in the neighborhood where Lebanese immigrants settled in Minneapolis around the 1880s and 1890s. By the Northeaster's account, some began as peddlers supplied on credit by early merchants, then opened groceries, trucking companies, restaurants and bars. Lebanese families in Northeast went on to run Minneapolis businesses such as Jacob's 101, which was open until 2005, along with Ray J's and Nye's.
The menu is home cooking, including hummus and baba ghannuj, spinach pie, kabobs and baklava.
keyFacts: 1936: Emily Awaijane arrived in the United States.
1973: Opened the deli at 641 University Ave. NE.
Family owned, by its own description.

institutions.name: Kahlil Gibran Memorial Garden
institutions.location: 3100 Massachusetts Ave. NW, Rock Creek Park, Washington, D.C.
body: On May 24, 1991, President George H. W. Bush dedicated a memorial garden to Kahlil Gibran on Massachusetts Avenue in Washington. He noted that cedars of Lebanon would someday shade the memorial, a reminder of the trees near Gibran's birthplace.

The memorial was sponsored by the Kahlil Gibran Centennial Foundation. In his remarks the President thanked Bill Baroody for his leadership and Sheryl Ameen, among others, for their work on the project. He credited Representative Mary Rose Oakar's sponsorship and saluted the actor Jamie Farr; Lebanon's ambassador was among the guests. The President and Barbara Bush were honorary co-chairs of the dedication committee.

The garden was designed by the architecture firm Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum, with a bronze sculpture of Gibran by Gordon S. Kray. Visitors cross a footbridge into the garden, which has a marble wall inscribed about Gibran's life and work, limestone benches carved with his words, an upper plaza and a fountain. Inscriptions include "Work is Love Made Visible," and the memorial was "Presented to the People of the United States." The National Park Service lists it as part of Rock Creek Park.
keyFacts: May 24, 1991: Dedicated by President George H. W. Bush.
Sponsor: Kahlil Gibran Centennial Foundation.
Sculptor: Gordon S. Kray; architects: Hellmuth, Obata & Kassabaum.
Listed by the National Park Service as part of Rock Creek Park.
institutions.connectToWork: Which public places in your own area show who is honored there? Who is missing, and what would you learn by asking how a memorial came to be built?

institutions.name: Lebanese Physically Handicapped Union
aliases: Lebanese Union for People with Physical Disabilities
institutions.location: Lebanon, national. Not a Minnesota resource
body: A small group of disabled women and men founded the union in mid-1981, during Lebanon's civil war. Its aim, according to a 2003 Oxfam account, was to mobilize disabled people and challenge their marginalization, not to provide services. Zero Project describes it today as a grassroots, non-sectarian group led by people with disabilities, which has worked to move policy from charity toward rights and inclusion.

Its work has included bringing displaced disabled people into its activities during the war and taking part in emergency relief in south Lebanon; monitoring elections and mobilizing voters in 1992, 1996 and 1998; joining an August 1998 march in Beirut for a disability rights bill; and sending members to the 1995 UN women's conference in Beijing. In June 1998, three disabled men won municipal council seats.
WISE Muslim Women's profile gives about 1,100 members and branches around the country, with no date. We could not find a current program list, or any tie to the United States or Minnesota.
keyFacts: 1981: Founded during the civil war.
1992, 1996, 1998: Monitored elections and mobilized voters.
1995: Members attended the UN women's conference in Beijing.
June 1998: Three disabled men won municipal seats.
institutions.connectToWork: When you describe disability services, do you frame them as charity or as rights? How would you find out which way the person would want them described?

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. We found no published research on disability among Lebanese Americans and no Minnesota study of Lebanese families. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) reports that 13.0 percent of Lebanese Minnesotans have a disability (plus or minus 4.3) and 10.5 percent of those under 65 (plus or minus 4.6); the margins are wide, and Compass says at least 12 percent of Minnesotans statewide have a disability. What follows comes from reports about Lebanon itself, gathered under very different conditions from those in Minnesota, and it may fit any one family loosely or not at all. Lebanese Minnesotans include Maronite and Antiochian Orthodox families, which are well documented, as well as people of other faiths or none, recent arrivals and families several generations on. Minnesota sources do not document Muslim or Druze congregations. Broader Arab American studies are on the Arabic-speaking page.
questions: What words do you and your family use to describe this, in English, Arabic or French? Which words would you like me to use?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it to you, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
How do you understand what is going on? If you want to tell me how it came about, I am glad to hear it, and you do not have to. Is that all right?
Who do you want involved in decisions: family, friends, a faith leader, or no one? Who would you rather I not include?
Who helps with care now? What would make that easier, and would you like to hear about respite or paid care supports?
Would you like your faith community involved in any of this, or would you rather keep it separate?
Are you worried about who might hear about this? Would it help if I explained who will see this information?
Which language do you prefer for this conversation? If you want an Arabic interpreter, do you have a preference about dialect, or about someone from outside your social circle?
What would a good life look like for you in five years?

context.heading: What a 2018 evidence review reports about Lebanon
body: A 2018 review by Éilís Combaz for the K4D program at the Institute of Development Studies summarized evidence about Lebanon, not Lebanese Americans. It found that views of disability there often rely on charitable or medical approaches rather than social or rights-based ones, and that stigma and prejudice are common, especially toward people with intellectual or mental disabilities. It describes a heavy care burden on family caregivers and limited, poorly enforced legal protections. It also says disability in Lebanon is under-researched, and that disabled people and their supporters have long experience of activism.

sources.label: Combaz (2018), Situation of Persons with Disabilities in Lebanon, K4D Helpdesk Report

context.heading: Two studies of families in Lebanon
body: Obeid and Daou presented a study of 161 mothers in Lebanon, 65 of them mothers of autistic children, in a 2014 conference abstract. It reports significant differences in well-being between the groups. Perceived social support did not track with well-being, and the authors suggest that may be because support in raising any child is commonly available in Lebanese families there. They also say parents of autistic children do not get adequate government support. It is one small study and a short abstract.

In 2022 the Norwegian Refugee Council, Oxfam and Solidarités International surveyed 292 families in Lebanon, each with a disabled member, during the country's economic crisis. The sample includes refugee families. Their report says caring for relatives often makes paid work unrealistic and that families take on debt or sell assets to pay for care. Conditions in Minnesota differ.

sources.label: Obeid and Daou (2014), INSAR conference abstract
Norwegian Refugee Council (2022), "Behind the curtain: life with disabilities in Lebanon"

context.heading: Disabled people organizing in Lebanon
body: Disabled people in Lebanon have led their own rights work for decades. The Lebanese Physically Handicapped Union began in 1981, in wartime, to mobilize disabled people rather than provide services. Nawaf Kabbara ran for Lebanon's parliament in 1996 and leads international disability bodies today. An activist quoted by the Norwegian Refugee Council in 2022, Fayez Oukacha, said, "People with disabilities are often seen as victims," and that policymakers design solutions without asking disabled people. Describing services as rights and supports, not charity, fits what these advocates have asked for, though the person in front of you may see it differently.

sources.label: Abou-Habib (2003), Humanitarian Exchange 13
International Disability Alliance, "Governance"
Norwegian Refugee Council (2022)

context.heading: Preparing to talk with someone
body: Do not infer religion from a surname, or assume that religion shapes how someone sees disability. Ask about language, since people may use English, Arabic or French or several of them, and ask whether an interpreter should come from outside the person's social circle. Ask early whether caregiver supports would help, and explain confidentiality in plain terms, without assuming anyone will be reluctant to disclose.

sources.label: Sahan Journal, "Lebanese Minnesotans sad, angry as Israel attacks homeland" (Oct. 22, 2024)
Combaz (2018), K4D Helpdesk Report

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no study of disability among Lebanese Americans or Lebanese Minnesotans. We found no documented Arabic disability terms specific to Lebanese speakers, though Lebanese groups have used both older "handicapped" wording and newer "persons with disabilities" wording. We found nothing documenting spiritual, fate-based or family-honor explanations, traditional healing, gender roles in disability decisions, or immigration-related fears among Lebanese families, so none are offered here. We found no Minnesota disability resource specific to Lebanese people, and no documented Lebanese American disability self-advocate. Lakkis and Kabbara are both based in Lebanon.

sources.label: Combaz (2018), K4D Helpdesk Report

organizations.intro: Lebanese immigrants began arriving in Minnesota in the late 1880s and 1890s, settling first in Northeast Minneapolis, on St. Paul's West Side and in Mankato. Sahan Journal, citing the 2022 American Community Survey, reported an estimated 8,000 Minnesotans with Lebanese ancestry, about 800 of them born in Lebanon. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) gives a 2024 single-year total of 10,066 (plus or minus 3,576), which it calls its most accurate estimate of size. These are survey estimates of people who chose to report that ancestry, and advocates say the survey undercounts Arab Americans. Among the groups with a public record we could open, Lebanese Minnesotans organize through parishes, family businesses and Arab American arts groups. We did not find a Minnesota Lebanese newspaper or radio program, a Lebanese-specific social-service agency, or any Lebanese Muslim or Druze institution in the state, which is a limit of the public record and not evidence that none exist. In 2024 Sahan Journal described a student following WhatsApp groups and a professor relying on the Lebanese press for news from home; that describes those people and no one else. The list is not complete. These are starting points for learning, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.name: Holy Family Maronite Catholic Church
entries.purpose: A Maronite parish begun in 1918 by Lebanese settlers on St. Paul's West Side. It moved from East Robie Street to Mendota Heights in 2009. It listed a fall festival on September 12, 2026, and a youth summer camp.

entries.name: St. George Antiochian Orthodox Church
entries.purpose: Founded in 1913 on St. Paul's West Side by Syrian and Lebanese immigrants, and in West St. Paul since 1974, when it held its first service there; the hall was built during 1973. By its own account the parish includes descendants of those families, immigrant families from Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Palestine, other Eastern Orthodox members and converts. It holds the Mid East Fest, most recently on July 18–19, 2026.
entries.linkLabel: Mid East Fest, the parish's festival site

entries.name: Mizna
entries.location: St. Paul, 2446 University Avenue West, Suite 115
entries.purpose: Founded in 1999 by Kathryn Haddad and Saleh Abudayyeh, it presents art, writing and film by Arab and Southwest Asian and North African artists. It publishes the print journal Mizna twice a year and runs the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival, begun in 2003. It is not a Lebanese organization, though Haddad's own family history includes migration from Lebanon.

entries.name: New Arab American Theater Works
entries.purpose: Makes theater, music and cultural work for, by and about Southwest Asian, North African and Muslim Americans, with play development, a drum ensemble and workshops. Its project The Hour of Separation, led by Kathryn Haddad, gathered stories of Lebanese who came to Minnesota about a century ago, with state cultural heritage funding for Lebanese and Syrian migration work.

entries.name: Yalla Count MENA In! Minnesota
entries.location: National campaign with a Minnesota page
entries.purpose: A coalition led by the Arab American Institute Foundation that seeks accurate counts of Middle Eastern and North African people, with Mizna among its Minnesota partners. Its page, drawing on 2013–2017 Census Bureau estimates, says Somali and Lebanese roots are the largest parts of the state's Arab American population and estimates that population at 108,553, adjusted for under-reporting. Useful if you collect or report on this data.

entries.name: Arab Student Association, University of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A campus group for Arab students, started in 2020 or 2021, that lists social and cultural events for 2025 and 2026. It is not specific to Lebanese students.

entries.name: Zakia Deli
entries.purpose: Opened in 2007 by David Maalouf with his mother, Zakia, whose name and recipes it carries, after his father's death. The menu mixes Lebanese, Greek and American dishes. Racket covered it in March 2025. Call before you go, since the listings we saw give different hours.

entries.name: American Task Force on Lebanon
entries.location: Washington, DC, 1100 Connecticut Avenue NW, Suite 1050
entries.purpose: Describes itself as a non-sectarian, non-partisan nonprofit educating policymakers and the public about US-Lebanon relations. It has been active since the mid-1980s, holds an annual dinner and runs internship and rising-leaders programs.

entries.name: Maronite Eparchy of Our Lady of Lebanon
entries.location: Based in St. Louis, Missouri, with a cathedral in Los Angeles
entries.purpose: The Maronite diocese serving Maronite Catholics from California to Ohio, including the St. Maron and Holy Family parishes in Minnesota. As of October 2026 its bishop is A. Elias Zaidan, appointed in 2013.

entries.name: Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America
entries.purpose: Oversees Antiochian parishes in the United States and Canada, including St. George in West St. Paul. Metropolitan Saba (Isper) was elected in February 2023 and enthroned that May.

entries.name: Leaders Advancing & Helping Communities
entries.purpose: Founded in 1982 as an athletic organization, it now offers food, health, behavioral health, workforce and education services in Southeast Michigan, plus a scholarship for Michigan students. A scholarship listing filed under the name Lebanese American Heritage Club now carries this group's name and says Lebanese heritage is not required, so do not treat it as a Lebanese heritage club.

entries.name: Arab American Institute
entries.purpose: Works on voting, census data, civil rights and immigration for Arab Americans, including Lebanese Americans, and publishes polling, most recently a national poll of likely voters in October 2026.

entries.name: American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee
entries.purpose: Describes itself as the largest Arab American grassroots organization. It offers legal help and takes discrimination complaints, and it was active in federal court over device seizures at borders in October 2026.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Covers Minnesota's immigrant communities in English. It reported on Lebanese Minnesotans' responses to the 2024 war in Lebanon.

entries.name: Northeaster
entries.purpose: Covers the neighborhood, including the history, churches and businesses of Lebanese Northeast. Its site was updating in October 2026.

entries.name: The Arab American News
entries.purpose: A bilingual paper covering the Arab world and Arab American communities, with a history its site puts at 39 years.

entries.name: LBCI
entries.type: Television and online, based in Lebanon
entries.purpose: A Lebanese private network with news in Arabic and English. The Media Ownership Monitor lists it among channels held by prominent Lebanese families. Read any Lebanese outlet knowing that ownership shapes coverage.

entries.name: MTV Lebanon
entries.type: Television and online, based in Lebanon
entries.purpose: A Lebanese private channel in Arabic. The Media Ownership Monitor says it was shut down by the authorities in 2002; it has since returned.

entries.name: Al Jadeed

entries.purpose: A Lebanese private channel in Arabic. The Media Ownership Monitor says it was temporarily shut down by the authorities in 1997.
